claim: CHD4 is essential for fusion-positive rhabdomyosarcoma (FP-RMS) survival.
source: Previously, we observed that CHD4 silencing leads to FP-RMS cell death in vitro and tumor regression in vivo (Böhm et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Böhm et al., 2016) demonstrating CHD4 silencing effects on FP-RMS.

claim: FP-RMS is particularly sensitive to CHD4 amongst all NuRD subunits for survival.
source: FP-RMS is particularly dependent on CHD4, amongst all NuRD subunits, for survival
evidence: Supported by CRISPR screen data showing CHD4 knockout had stronger effects than other NuRD subunits.

claim: CHD4 knockout decreased RH4 cell proliferation below 75% threshold with 4 out of 5 sgRNAs.
source: For CHD4, HDAC1, and RBBP4 knockouts, 4 out of 5 sgRNAs and for GATAD2A 3 out of 5 sgRNAs decreased RH4 cell proliferation below the 75% threshold.
evidence: Directly stated results from CRISPR screen experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MBD and MTA protein knockouts did not significantly alter RH4 cell proliferation at day 12.
source: Notably, knockouts of the MBD and MTA proteins, both core and mutually exclusive members of NuRD (Allen et al., 2013), as well as of LSD1 did not significantly alter RH4 cell proliferation at day 12.
evidence: Experimental results from CRISPR screen with citation to NuRD complex composition.

claim: CHD4 single knockout affected FP-RMS cell proliferation more than other NuRD members as single or double knockouts.
source: However, depletion of NuRD members as single or double knockouts affected FP-RMS cell proliferation to a lesser extent than CHD4 single knockout (median of KO/Control ratio obtained with the five sgRNAs tested: CHD3–98%, CHD4–51%, MBD2–102%, MBD3–107%, MBD2/3–68%, HDAC1–71%, HDAC2–89%, HDAC1/2–59%, MTA1–109%, MTA2–98%, MTA3–92%, RBBP4–66%, RBBP7–82%, GATAD2A – 63%, GATAD2B – 80%, GATAD2A/B – 65%, LSD1–88%; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of median KO/Control ratios from CRISPR screen data.

claim: RBBP4 depletion reduced FP-RMS cell proliferation but did not induce cell death.
source: Confirming the CRISPR screen, RBBP4 depletion by shRNA reduced FP-RMS cell proliferation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and F). However, unlike CHD4 and P3F silencing, RBBP4 knockdown did not induce FP-RMS cell death (Figure 1C and D)
evidence: Experimental data from shRNA knockdown experiments shown in figures.

claim: RBBP4 knockdown did not influence the expression of 5 out of 6 selected P3F target genes.
source: nor did it influence the expression of 5 out of 6 selected P3F target genes (Figure 1E,F and G).
evidence: qPCR data showing gene expression levels after RBBP4 knockdown.

claim: CHD4 does not recognize a specific DNA sequence.
source: CHD4 does not recognize a specific DNA sequence (Bouazoune et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from previous publication (Bouazoune et al., 2002).

claim: CHD4 is recruited to the genome by its interaction partners.
source: Instead, it is recruited to the genome by its interaction partners.
evidence: Logical inference based on the lack of DNA sequence specificity and established knowledge of chromatin remodeler recruitment mechanisms.

claim: 103 potential CHD4 interactors were identified with fold change of at least two and saint score higher than 0.6.
source: Considering a fold change of at least two and a saint score higher than 0.6, a total of 103 potential interactors were identified (Figure 2B).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data analysis results with specific statistical thresholds.

claim: 59% of CHD4 putative interactors have been detected in previous publications.
source: To evaluate the quality of our interactome we compared it to reported interaction partners available on BioGRID 3.5 (Oughtred et al., 2019) and observed that 59% of our putative interactors have also been detected in previous publications (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Comparison with published interaction data from BioGRID database.

claim: CHD4 interactome is enriched for epigenetic regulators of gene expression.
source: Gene ontology analysis of the putative interactors was performed using the Metascape online platform (http://metascape.org/) and revealed an enrichment for epigenetic regulators of gene expression (Figure 2C).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis results from mass spectrometry data.

claim: The majority of CHD4 interactors are involved in transcription regulation and belong to chromatin remodeling or modifying complexes.
source: After further categorization of the potential interactors, we confirmed that the majority are involved in transcription regulation and belong to chromatin remodeling or modifying complexes (Figure 2D).
evidence: Categorization of mass spectrometry-identified interactors.

claim: NuRD subunits (excluding RBBP4/7) were identified as high confidence CHD4 interactors.
source: Expectedly, the NuRD subunits, excluding RBBP4/7, were identified as high confidence interactors (Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data showing protein-protein interactions.

claim: BRD4 is essential for the regulation of the aberrant P3F gene expression signature in FP-RMS.
source: Since BRD4 is essential for the regulation of the aberrant P3F gene expression signature in FP-RMS (Gryder et al., 2017)
evidence: Cited from previous publication (Gryder et al., 2017).

claim: Flag immunoprecipitation of CHD4 pulled down BRD4 and all tested NuRD subunits including RBBP4.
source: Flag immunoprecipitation of CHD4 was able to pull-down BRD4 as well as all subunits of NuRD tested, including RBBP4, which was not identified in our interactome studies (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experimental data.

claim: BRD4 immunoprecipitation coprecipitated CHD4, HDAC2, and MTA2.
source: Interestingly, the Flag pull-down of BRD4 not only coprecipitated CHD4 but also HDAC2 and MTA2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G)
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experimental data.

claim: BRD4 interacts with CHD4 in the context of NuRD complex.
source: suggesting that BRD4 interacts with CHD4 in the context of NuRD.
evidence: Inference from co-immunoprecipitation data showing BRD4 pulls down multiple NuRD components.

claim: BRD4 immunoprecipitation did not pull down HDAC1 or RBBP4.
source: However, BRD4 immunoprecipitation was not able to pull-down HDAC1 nor RBBP4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and H)
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experimental data.

claim: CHD4 ChIP-seq signal correlated with RBBP4, HDAC2, MTA2, and BRD4 in the genome.
source: A correlation matrix generated from the ChIP-seq data (Figure 3A) demonstrated that CHD4 co-occurs with its interactors RBBP4, HDAC2, MTA2, and BRD4 in the genome.
evidence: ChIP-seq correlation analysis data.

claim: CHD4 ChIP-seq signal correlated with P3F and enhancer marks H3K27ac and H3K4me1, but not with H3K27me3.
source: Strikingly, CHD4 ChIP-seq signal also correlated with the one of P3F and the enhancer marks H3K27ac and H3K4me1, but not with H3K27me3.
evidence: ChIP-seq correlation analysis data.

claim: CHD4, RBBP4, HDAC2, and MTA2 mainly localized to enhancers.
source: The overlay of the ChIP-seq signals of CHD4, RBBP4, HDAC2, and MTA2 on the chromatin states map (Ernst et al., 2011) confirmed that these NuRD members mainly localized to enhancers (Figure 3B).
evidence: ChIP-seq data overlaid on chromatin state maps.

claim: RBBP4, HDAC2, and MTA2 showed additional strong prevalence at active promoters in contrast to CHD4.
source: Interestingly, RBBP4, HDAC2, and MTA2, in contrast to CHD4, showed an additional strong prevalence at active promoters.
evidence: ChIP-seq data analysis showing differential localization patterns.

claim: Roughly 66% of locations shared amongst HDAC2, RBBP4 and MTA2 did not co-localize with CHD4.
source: The overlap of the genomic locations of the NuRD components (Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 1) showed that roughly 66% of the locations shared amongst HDAC2, RBBP4 and MTA2 (8901 out of 13,5000) did not co-localize with CHD4
evidence: ChIP-seq peak overlap analysis with quantitative results.

claim: A CHD4-free NuRD complex (NuRD-only) and a NuRD complex containing CHD4 (CHD4/NuRD) exist in FP-RMS.
source: suggesting the presence of a CHD4-free NuRD complex (NuRD-only) and a NuRD complex containing CHD4 (CHD4/NuRD).
evidence: Inference from ChIP-seq peak overlap data showing distinct localization patterns.

claim: NuRD-only peaks were frequently found near transcription start sites and in promoter regions.
source: The NuRD-only peaks (n = 8,901) were frequently found in the vicinity of transcription start sites (TSSs) and in promoter regions (Figure 3D)
evidence: ChIP-seq peak distribution analysis relative to genomic features.

claim: CHD4/NuRD peaks predominantly located distally to TSSs and to intronic or intergenic regions.
source: in contrast to CHD4/NuRD peaks (n = 4,599) which predominantly located distally to TSSs and to intronic or intergenic regions (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: ChIP-seq peak distribution analysis relative to genomic features.

claim: NuRD-only locations were characterized by the presence of RNA Pol 2 and the promoter mark H3K4me3.
source: In line with these results, NuRD-only locations were characterized by the presence of RNA Pol 2 and the promoter mark H3K4me3
evidence: ChIP-seq data showing co-localization of different factors.

claim: CHD4/NuRD sites were richer in enhancer-related histone marks H3K4me1 and H3K27ac, as well as in BRD4.
source: while CHD4/NuRD sites were richer in the enhancer-related histone marks H3K4me1 and H3K27ac, as well as in BRD4 (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: ChIP-seq data showing enrichment of specific histone marks and factors.

claim: Both NuRD-only and CHD4/NuRD locations were sensitive to DNase I digestion, suggesting open chromatin conformation.
source: As expected for active regions, both NuRD-only and CHD4/NuRD locations were sensitive to DNase I digestion, suggesting an open chromatin conformation at these sites (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: DNase I hypersensitivity assay data indicating chromatin accessibility.

claim: CHD4/NuRD regions were associated with processes involved in muscle development more frequently than NuRD-only regions.
source: After categorization of all biological processes found, we observed that CHD4/NuRD regions were associated with processes involved in the regulation of muscle development and other myogenic processes more frequently than NuRD-only regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis of genomic regions.

claim: NuRD-only locations were correlated with regulation of genes involved in general processes such as gene expression and mRNA metabolism.
source: NuRD-only locations were instead correlated with the regulation of genes involved in general processes such as gene expression and mRNA metabolism (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis of genomic regions.

claim: 42% of P3F locations were also bound by CHD4/NuRD.
source: The overlap between P3F and CHD4/NuRD ChIP-seq signal (Figure 4A and Figure 4—source data 1) showed that 42% of P3F locations were also bound by CHD4/NuRD (P3F+CHD4/NuRD regions; 1,538 out of 3,696 peaks).
evidence: ChIP-seq peak overlap analysis with quantitative results.

claim: P3F+CHD4/NuRD sites were richer in H3K27ac and BRD4 compared to P3F-only locations.
source: Interestingly, P3F+CHD4/NuRD sites, in comparison with P3F-only locations (n = 2,158), were richer in the enhancer mark H3K27ac and BRD4
evidence: ChIP-seq data comparison between different genomic regions.

claim: P3F+CHD4/NuRD sites displayed a more open chromatin conformation than P3F-only locations.
source: and displayed a more open conformation as shown by DNase I hypersensitivity assays (Figure 4B).
evidence: DNase I hypersensitivity assay data comparing different genomic regions.

claim: P3F+CHD4/NuRD-regulated genes were significantly higher expressed than P3F-only-regulated genes.
source: Analysis of the expression of the nearest genes, within topological associated domains (TADs), associated with P3F-only, P3F+CHD4/NuRD and CHD4/NuRD-only binding sites (Figure 4—source data 1) revealed that P3F+CHD4/NuRD-regulated genes were significantly higher expressed than P3F-only-regulated genes (Figure 4C).
evidence: RNA-seq gene expression data linked to ChIP-seq binding sites.

claim: HDAC2, RBBP4, and MTA2 were present in 784 out of 810 super-enhancers predicted in RH4 cells.
source: Regarding the presence of CHD4/NuRD at SEs, we observed that HDAC2, RBBP4, and MTA2 were present in a total of 784 out of the 810 SEs predicted according to H3K27ac abundancy in RH4 cells (Figure 4D and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: ChIP-seq data analysis at super-enhancer regions.

claim: 595 out of 784 super-enhancers with NuRD subunits were co-bound by CHD4.
source: Of these 784 SEs, 595 were co-bound by CHD4 (Figure 4D and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: ChIP-seq data analysis at super-enhancer regions.

claim: 90% of P3F-occupied super-enhancers were co-bound by CHD4/NuRD.
source: Remarkably, analysis of the SEs occupied by P3F in RH4 cells demonstrated that 90% (407 out of 452) were co-bound by CHD4/NuRD (Figure 4E and Figure 4—source data 1)
evidence: ChIP-seq peak overlap analysis at super-enhancer regions.

claim: CHD4 silencing caused a drastic decrease in super-enhancer accessibility.
source: Strikingly, we observed a drastic decrease in SE accessibility upon CHD4 silencing (Figure 4F)
evidence: DNase I hypersensitivity assay data after CHD4 knockdown.

claim: CHD4 is necessary for the maintenance of DNA accessibility at super-enhancers.
source: suggesting that this chromatin remodeler is necessary for the maintenance of DNA accessibility at these locations.
evidence: Inference from DNase I hypersensitivity data showing reduced accessibility after CHD4 depletion.

claim: CHD4 knockdown reduced P3F binding to super-enhancers.
source: Using spike-in normalization, we observed that CHD4 knockdown reduced P3F binding to SEs (Figure 4F).
evidence: ChIP-seq data with spike-in normalization after CHD4 knockdown.

claim: CHD4 depletion caused an increase and spread of H3K27ac at super-enhancers.
source: In line with HDAC2 displacement, we also observed that CHD4 depletion caused an increase and spread of H3K27ac as well as an increase of BRD4 binding to SEs (Figure 4F).
evidence: ChIP-seq data for histone marks after CHD4 knockdown.

claim: CHD4 depletion caused an increase of BRD4 binding to super-enhancers.
source: In line with HDAC2 displacement, we also observed that CHD4 depletion caused an increase and spread of H3K27ac as well as an increase of BRD4 binding to SEs (Figure 4F).
evidence: ChIP-seq data for BRD4 after CHD4 knockdown.

claim: CHD4 silencing led to 2,195 upregulated genes and 2,848 downregulated genes after 48 hours.
source: We observed that silencing of either protein led to an equal number of up- and downregulated genes (after 48hrs of CHD4 silencing 2,195 genes were upregulated and 2,848 downregulated, while upon 48hrs of P3F silencing 1,827 were upregulated and 1,700 downregulated; false discovery rate - 1%, fold change ≥25%, Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: RNA-seq differential gene expression analysis data.

claim: Both CHD4 and P3F depletion preferentially affected super-enhancer-mediated gene expression.
source: Interestingly, both CHD4 and P3F depletion preferentially affected SE-mediated gene expression (Figure 5B).
evidence: RNA-seq data analysis comparing effects on genes associated with super-enhancers versus typical enhancers.

claim: CHD4 silencing influenced the expression of 28% of P3F target genes at 48 hours.
source: At 48hrs, CHD4 silencing influenced the expression of 28% of P3F target genes (541 protein coding genes were co-upregulated upon CHD4 or P3F depletion and 449 were co-downregulated, Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: RNA-seq data analysis showing overlap of CHD4 and P3F regulated genes.

claim: CHD4 does not regulate the expression of P3F itself.
source: Importantly, we observed that CHD4 does not regulate the expression of P3F itself (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D)
evidence: Western blot and qPCR data showing P3F levels after CHD4 knockdown.

claim: CHD4 depletion decreased RNA Pol 2 binding at TSSs and TESs of genes co-downregulated by CHD4 and P3F.
source: To this end, we examined total RNA Pol 2 binding in the presence and absence of CHD4 by ChIP-seq, using spike-in normalization, and observed that depletion of CHD4 decreased RNA Pol 2 binding at TSSs and transcription end sites (TESs) of genes co-downregulated by CHD4 and P3F suppression (n = 449, Figure 5F).
evidence: ChIP-seq data for RNA Pol 2 after CHD4 knockdown with spike-in normalization.

claim: CHD4 expression is generally higher in tumors than in normal tissue.
source: In agreement, analysis of the R2 gene expression database (r2.aml.nl) revealed that CHD4 expression is generally higher in tumors (269 datasets) than in normal tissue (38 datasets; Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Gene expression database analysis comparing tumor and normal tissue.

claim: Loss of CHD4 impaired tumor cell viability in >92% of cancer cell lines in both RNAi and CRISPR datasets.
source: We observed that loss of CHD4 impaired tumor cell viability in >92% of the cancer cell lines used in both datasets (in the combined RNAi database, 627 out of 712 cancer cell lines were sensitive to CHD4 silencing and in the CRISPR dataset 552 out of 558 cancer cell lines were affected by CHD4 knockout).
evidence: Analysis of large-scale cancer dependency databases.

claim: All tumor types represented in both RNAi and CRISPR datasets were sensitive to CHD4 depletion.
source: All tumor types represented in both datasets were sensitive to CHD4 depletion (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Analysis of cancer dependency databases across tumor types.

claim: CHD4 had the lowest dependency scores among SNF2-like chromatin remodelers and BRD4 in cancer databases.
source: In both databases loss of SRCAP, EP400, INO80 and BRD4 induced a general impairment of tumor cell viability, however, the lowest dependency scores were observed for CHD4 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Comparative analysis of dependency scores across different chromatin remodelers.

claim: The NuRD complex combines chromatin remodeling and histone deacetylase activity.
source: This complex combines both chromatin remodeling (carried out by CHD3/4/5) and histone deacetylase (attributed to HDAC1/2) activity.
evidence: Established knowledge about NuRD complex composition and function.

claim: The NuRD complex was originally defined as a transcription repressor.
source: The NuRD, partially due to its deacetylase activity, was originally defined as a transcription repressor (Xue et al., 1998)
evidence: Cited from original characterization of NuRD complex.

claim: There is increasing evidence that NuRD might mediate both positive and negative regulation of gene expression.
source: however there is increasing evidence suggesting that it might mediate both positive and negative regulation of gene expression (Bornelöv et al., 2018; Günther et al., 2013; Hosokawa et al., 2013; Miccio et al., 2010).
evidence: Multiple citations to recent publications showing dual roles of NuRD.

claim: PAX3-FOXO1 is the product of the most common chromosomal translocation in FP-RMS, t(2;13)(q35;q14).
source: PAX3-FOXO1, the product of the most common chromosomal translocation observed, t(2;13)(q35;q14) (De Giovanni et al., 2009; Shern et al., 2014)
evidence: Cited from publications characterizing FP-RMS genetics.

claim: PAX3-FOXO1 drives tumor development by binding to enhancers and super-enhancers to activate aberrant gene expression.
source: drives tumor development by binding to enhancers and super-enhancers to activate an aberrant gene expression signature (Cao et al., 2010; Gryder et al., 2017; Khan et al., 1999).
evidence: Multiple citations to publications characterizing PAX3-FOXO1 function.

claim: FP-RMS is dependent on its unique fusion genes.
source: Since FP-RMS is dependent on its unique fusion genes (Bernasconi et al., 1996)
evidence: Cited from publication demonstrating fusion gene dependency.

claim: CHD4 co-regulates the expression of a subset of PAX3-FOXO1 target genes.
source: Recently, we demonstrated that the NuRD complex subunit and SNF2-like ATPase CHD4 (chromodomain-helicase-DNA-binding protein 4) is essential for FP-RMS survival and co-regulates the expression of a subset of PAX3-FOXO1 target genes (Böhm et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous publication by the authors.

claim: CHD4 generates a chromatin architecture permissive for PAX3-FOXO1 binding at super-enhancers.
source: Mechanistically, NuRD complex containing CHD4 localizes to super-enhancers where CHD4 generates a chromatin architecture permissive for the binding of the tumor driver and fusion protein PAX3-FOXO1, allowing downstream transcription of its oncogenic program.
evidence: Experimental data from ChIP-seq and DNase assays showing CHD4's role in chromatin accessibility and P3F binding.

claim: CHD4 depletion removes HDAC2 from chromatin, leading to increased and spread histone acetylation.
source: Moreover, CHD4 depletion removes HDAC2 from the chromatin, leading to an increase and spread of histone acetylation
evidence: ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data showing HDAC2 displacement and H3K27ac changes after CHD4 knockdown.

claim: CHD4 depletion prevents the positioning of RNA Polymerase 2 at promoters, impeding transcription initiation.
source: and prevents the positioning of RNA Polymerase 2 at promoters impeding transcription initiation.
evidence: ChIP-seq data showing reduced RNA Pol 2 at TSSs after CHD4 knockdown.

claim: CHD4 is a general cancer vulnerability based on genome-wide cancer dependency databases.
source: Strikingly, analysis of genome-wide cancer dependency databases identifies CHD4 as a general cancer vulnerability.
evidence: Analysis of Combined RNAi and CRISPR cancer dependency databases.

claim: CHD4, a classically defined repressor, functions as a positive regulator of transcription and super-enhancer accessibility.
source: Our findings describe CHD4, a classically defined repressor, as positive regulator of transcription and super-enhancer accessibility
evidence: Experimental data showing CHD4's role in maintaining open chromatin and promoting gene expression at super-enhancers.

claim: CHD4 represents a broad tumor susceptibility and promising drug target for cancer therapy.
source: as well as establish this remodeler as an unexpected broad tumor susceptibility and promising drug target for cancer therapy.
evidence: Inference from cancer dependency database analysis showing broad essentiality across tumor types.

claim: Chromatin remodelers regulate gene expression by controlling DNA accessibility to the transcriptional machinery.
source: Chromatin remodelers regulate gene expression by controlling DNA accessibility to the transcriptional machinery at regulatory sites (Clapier and Cairns, 2009).
evidence: Established knowledge about chromatin remodeler function with citation.

claim: SNF2-like ATPases use energy from ATP hydrolysis to assemble, evict and move nucleosomes or exchange histone variants.
source: The remodeling process is conducted by SNF2-like ATPases, usually working as subunits of multiprotein complexes, which use energy drawn from ATP hydrolysis to assemble, evict and move nucleosomes or exchange histone variants (Clapier et al., 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge about chromatin remodeler mechanism with citation.

claim: Super-enhancers regulate cell identity during normal development and drive high expression of oncogenes in cancer.
source: During normal development, SEs regulate cell identity while in cancer they drive high expression of oncogenes (Hnisz et al., 2013; Sengupta and George, 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge about super-enhancer function with citations.

claim: In FP-RMS, P3F drives tumorigenesis by creating and binding to super-enhancers to alter gene expression.
source: In FP-RMS, P3F drives tumorigenesis by creating and binding to SEs to alter gene expression (Gryder et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from previous publication characterizing P3F function in FP-RMS.

claim: CHD5 is preferentially expressed in neural and testicular tissues.
source: CHD5 was excluded from this screen due to its preferential expression in neural and testicular tissues (Kolla et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from publication characterizing CHD5 expression pattern.

claim: CHD5 is not expressed in RH4 cells based on RNA-seq data.
source: Indeed, RNA-seq data of RH4 cells demonstrated that CHD5 is not expressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: RNA-seq expression data for CHD5 in RH4 cells.

claim: Apart from MTA2, all other NuRD subunits tested are highly expressed in FP-RMS tumor tissue.
source: Apart from MTA2, all other NuRD subunits tested are highly expressed in FP-RMS tumor tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Microarray expression data from FP-RMS tumor samples.

claim: HDAC1/2 are redundant NuRD subunits.
source: The single knockouts as well as the double knockouts of the redundant NuRD subunits HDAC1/2 (Jurkin et al., 2011)
evidence: Cited from publication demonstrating HDAC1/2 redundancy.

claim: A specific HDAC1/2 inhibitor decreased FP-RMS proliferation and disrupted SE-driven gene expression.
source: In fact, a specific HDAC1/2 inhibitor was shown to decrease FP-RMS proliferation and disrupt SE-driven gene expression (Gryder et al., 2019b)
evidence: Cited from publication testing HDAC1/2 inhibitor effects.

claim: RBBP4 is present in other chromatin modifying complexes such as SIN3 and PRC2.
source: Yet, RBBP4 is also present in other chromatin modifying complexes, such as SIN3 and PRC2 (Allen et al., 2013)
evidence: Cited from publication characterizing RBBP4 complex associations.

claim: GATAD2 paralogs connect CHD4 to the MBD-GATAD2 dimer which binds to the HDAC-MTA-RBBP subcomplex.
source: These paralogs connect CHD4 to the MBD-GATAD2 dimer which binds to the HDAC-MTA-RBBP subcomplex, forming the NuRD complex.
evidence: Established knowledge about NuRD complex architecture based on structural studies.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of GATAD2A in mammalian cells pulls down CHD4 but no other NuRD component.
source: Interestingly, immunoprecipitation of GATAD2A in mammalian cells pulls-down CHD4 but no other NuRD component (Torrado et al., 2017)
evidence: Cited from publication characterizing GATAD2A interactions.

claim: In mouse embryonic stem cells in the absence of Mbd3, Chd4 remains associated with Gatad2b.
source: and in mouse embryonic stem cells in the absence of Mbd3 Chd4 remains associated with Gatad2b (Bornelöv et al., 2018)
evidence: Cited from publication studying NuRD complex composition in stem cells.

claim: MBD subunits are mutually exclusive members of NuRD and crucial for complex assembly.
source: Despite single knockouts of the MBD subunits, which are mutually exclusive members of the complex and crucial for the assembly NuRD (Zhang et al., 2016)
evidence: Cited from publication characterizing MBD role in NuRD assembly.

claim: CHD4 silencing had no influence on proliferation of human myoblasts and fibroblasts.
source: Extraordinarily, sensitivity to CHD4 depletion seems to be specific to cancer cells as we and others observed that silencing of this chromatin remodeler had no influence on proliferation of human myoblasts, fibroblasts (Böhm et al., 2016)
evidence: Cited from previous publication by the authors.

claim: CHD4 silencing had no influence on proliferation of non-transformed mammary epithelial cells (MCF10A).
source: non-transformed mammary epithelial cells (MCF10A) (D'Alesio et al., 2016)
evidence: Cited from publication testing CHD4 effects in normal cells.

claim: CHD4 silencing had no influence on proliferation of normal primary hematopoietic cells.
source: and normal primary hematopoietic cells (Heshmati et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from publication testing CHD4 effects in normal cells.

claim: In glioblastoma, CHD4 co-localizes with transcription factor ZFHX4 and co-regulates a subset of its target genes.
source: Besides FP-RMS, in glioblastoma, CHD4 co-localizes with the transcription factor ZFHX4 and co-regulates a subset of its target genes to maintain the tumor-initiating cell population (Chudnovsky et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from publication characterizing CHD4 function in glioblastoma.

claim: CHD4 has been implicated in the viability of breast cancer, acute myeloid leukemia, lung cancer, and colorectal cancer.
source: Besides FP-RMS, CHD4 has been implicated in the viability of other tumors such as breast cancer (D'Alesio et al., 2016), acute myeloid leukemia (Heshmati et al., 2016), lung cancer (Xu et al., 2016), and colorectal cancer (Xia et al., 2017).
evidence: Multiple citations to publications showing CHD4 role in different cancer types.

claim: CHD4 is involved in DNA-damage repair and genome integrity.
source: Nonetheless, the role of CHD4 in DNA-damage repair and genome integrity (Qi et al., 2016; Smeenk et al., 2010) should be further explored in the context of general tumor sensitivity.
evidence: Cited from publications characterizing CHD4 role in DNA repair.

claim: Correlation between reduced HDAC activity, acetylation spreading and RNA Pol 2 depletion halting transcription initiation has been recently described.
source: Such correlation between reduced HDAC activity, acetylation spreading and RNA Pol 2 depletion halting transcription initiation has been recently described (Gryder et al., 2019a).
evidence: Cited from recent publication describing this mechanism.

claim: Both chromatin remodeling and histone deacetylation are core functions of NuRD required for expression of genes regulated by super-enhancers in FP-RMS.
source: These results confirm that both the remodeling activity and histone deacetylation are core functions of NuRD required for the expression of genes regulated by SEs in FP-RMS.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing effects of CHD4 depletion on chromatin accessibility, HDAC2 localization, and gene expression.

claim: NuRD regulates distinct biological processes according to its composition and location.
source: NuRD regulates distinct biological processes according to its composition and location
evidence: Gene ontology analysis showing different biological processes associated with CHD4/NuRD versus NuRD-only regions.

claim: NuRD-only peaks are associated with regulation of housekeeping processes.
source: NuRD-only peaks, including many promoter regions, were associated with the regulation of housekeeping processes
evidence: Gene ontology analysis of NuRD-only genomic regions.

claim: CHD4/NuRD locations are involved in regulation of cell-type specific processes characteristic of FP-RMS.
source: whereas CHD4/NuRD locations, predominantly found in enhancers, were involved in the regulation of cell-type specific processes characteristic of FP-RMS.
evidence: Gene ontology analysis of CHD4/NuRD genomic regions.

claim: Cell type-specific processes related to muscle development are mainly associated with P3F+CHD4/NuRD and P3F-only regions.
source: GREAT ontology analysis of the P3F-only, P3F+CHD4/NuRD and P3F-free CHD4/NuRD regions (CHD4/NuRD-only regions) demonstrated that cell type-specific processes related with muscle development, which are characteristic of FP-RMS, were mainly associated with P3F+CHD4/NuRD and P3F-only regions and absent from the top 15 enriched biological processes obtained for CHD4/NuRD-only regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis comparing different genomic region categories.

claim: CHD4 collaborates with P3F to activate gene expression partially by increasing RNA Pol 2 binding to TSSs.
source: Together, our observations imply that CHD4 regulates SE-mediated gene expression and that it collaborates with P3F to activate gene expression partially by increasing the binding of RNA Pol 2 to the TSSs.
evidence: Inference from RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data showing coordinated effects of CHD4 and P3F on gene expression and RNA Pol 2 positioning.

claim: CHD4 might collaborate with other chromatin remodeling complexes besides NuRD, such as SWI/SNF.
source: Additionally, our interactome studies suggest that CHD4 might collaborate with other chromatin remodeling complexes besides NuRD, such as SWI/SNF, and transcription regulators, like BRD4, to influence FP-RMS cell proliferation.
evidence: Inference from mass spectrometry interactome data showing SWI/SNF components as CHD4 interactors.

claim: The broad tumor dependency on CHD4 might be partially explained by its positive contribution to oncogenic transcription factor activity at super-enhancers.
source: We believe that this broad tumor dependency on CHD4 might be partially explained by its positive contribution to the activity of oncogenic transcription factors at super-enhancers.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental findings in FP-RMS and cancer dependency database analysis.

claim: The NuRD complex is a highly conserved and ubiquitously expressed multisubunit complex.
source: The nucleosome remodeling and histone deacetylase (NuRD) complex is a highly conserved and ubiquitously expressed multisubunit complex (Torchy et al., 2015)
evidence: Established knowledge about NuRD complex with citation.

claim: The NuRD complex plays an essential role during normal development and in tumorigenesis.
source: which plays an essential role during normal development as well as in tumorigenesis (Lai and Wade, 2011).
evidence: Established knowledge about NuRD function with citation.

claim: NuRD subunits assemble in a combinatorial fashion and variations in complex composition may reflect changes in its activity.
source: The NuRD subunits assemble in a combinatorial fashion and variations in the complex composition may reflect changes in its activity (Bowen et al., 2004).
evidence: Established knowledge about NuRD assembly with citation.

claim: Structural studies suggest NuRD is composed of two HDACs, two MTAs, four RBBPs and one MBD, GATAD2 and CHD subunits.
source: Currently, structural studies suggest that this complex is composed of two HDACs, two MTAs, four RBBPs and one MBD, GATAD2 and CHD subunits (Torchy et al., 2015; Torrado et al., 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge from structural studies with citations.

claim: FP-RMS is a rare pediatric sarcoma with a low mutational burden that exhibits features of skeletal myogenesis.
source: Fusion-positive rhabdomyosarcoma (FP-RMS) is a rare pediatric sarcoma with a low mutational burden that exhibits features of skeletal myogenesis (Shern et al., 2014).
evidence: Established knowledge about FP-RMS characteristics with citation.

claim: FP-RMS tumorigenesis is associated with chromosomal translocations resulting in expression of fusion oncogenic transcription factors.
source: Its tumorigenesis is associated with the presence of chromosomal translocations which result in the expression of fusion oncogenic transcription factors.
evidence: Established knowledge about FP-RMS molecular pathogenesis.

claim: CHD4 strongly interacts with chromatin through its histone binding domains.
source: Importantly, since CHD4 strongly interacts with chromatin through its histone binding domains (Mansfield et al., 2011)
evidence: Established knowledge about CHD4 chromatin binding with citation.

claim: Some CHD4 interactions identified in the interactome may be indirect and chromatin-mediated.
source: and nucleosome core particles are present in our interactome, we cannot exclude that some of the interactions identified here are indirect and chromatin-mediated.
evidence: Inference from the presence of nucleosome components in the interactome and known CHD4 chromatin binding properties.

claim: CHD4 is a nucleosome remodeler capable of moving nucleosomes along the DNA.
source: Since CHD4 is a nucleosome remodeler capable of moving nucleosomes along the DNA (Xue et al., 1998)
evidence: Established knowledge about CHD4 remodeling activity with citation.

claim: CHD4 might influence chromatin architecture at its binding sites.
source: we hypothesized that CHD4 might influence the chromatin architecture at its binding sites.
evidence: Hypothesis based on known CHD4 nucleosome remodeling activity.

claim: 35% of CHD4/NuRD locations identified in RH4 were also occupied by CHD4/NuRD in RH5 cells.
source: The presence of CHD4/NuRD at these 4,599 locations distal to TSSs identified in RH4 cells was confirmed in two other FP-RMS cell lines by performing ChIP-seq assays for CHD4, RBBP4, HDAC2, and MTA2 in RH5 and SCMC cells (35% and 54% of the 4,599 CHD4/NuRD locations identified in RH4 were also occupied by CHD4/NuRD in RH5 and SCMC cells, respectively; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: ChIP-seq data from multiple FP-RMS cell lines showing overlap of CHD4/NuRD binding sites.

claim: 54% of CHD4/NuRD locations identified in RH4 were also occupied by CHD4/NuRD in SCMC cells.
source: The presence of CHD4/NuRD at these 4,599 locations distal to TSSs identified in RH4 cells was confirmed in two other FP-RMS cell lines by performing ChIP-seq assays for CHD4, RBBP4, HDAC2, and MTA2 in RH5 and SCMC cells (35% and 54% of the 4,599 CHD4/NuRD locations identified in RH4 were also occupied by CHD4/NuRD in RH5 and SCMC cells, respectively; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: ChIP-seq data from multiple FP-RMS cell lines showing overlap of CHD4/NuRD binding sites.

claim: CHD4/NuRD co-localized with P3F in roughly 50% of P3F binding sites across three FP-RMS cell lines.
source: P3F and CHD4/NuRD locations were defined by the presence of ChIP-seq signal in at least two out of the three FP-RMS cell lines tested (RH4, RH5 and SCMC). Using this criterion, we observed that CHD4/NuRD co-localized with P3F in roughly 50% of P3F binding sites (778 out of 1,569; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: ChIP-seq data from three FP-RMS cell lines showing P3F and CHD4/NuRD co-localization.

claim: CHD4 silencing led to a moderate decrease in genome accessibility at P3F+CHD4/NuRD and CHD4/NuRD-only locations.
source: Similarly, at P3F+CHD4/NuRD locations (including enhancers and SEs) and CHD4/NuRD-only locations, CHD4 silencing led to a moderate decrease in genome accessibility (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: DNase I hypersensitivity assay data after CHD4 knockdown.

claim: A comparable reduction in P3F binding was observed at P3F+CHD4/NuRD locations after CHD4 knockdown.
source: A comparable reduction in P3F binding was also observed at P3F+CHD4/NuRD locations (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: ChIP-seq data for P3F after CHD4 knockdown.

claim: HDAC2 binding was reduced at ALK and CDH3 locations after CHD4 silencing.
source: To evaluate NuRD chromatin positioning upon CHD4 silencing, we performed ChIP-qPCR assays of HDAC2 at three P3F selected target locations and observed that HDAC2 binding was reduced at 2 of these locations (ALK and CDH3, Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR data for HDAC2 after CHD4 knockdown.

claim: ALK and CDH3 expression are reduced after CHD4 silencing but not ASS1.
source: Curiously, both ALK and CDH3 expression are reduced after CHD4 silencing but not the one of ASS1 (Figure 1G).
evidence: qPCR gene expression data after CHD4 knockdown.

claim: P3F silencing led to 1,827 upregulated genes and 1,700 downregulated genes after 48 hours.
source: We observed that silencing of either protein led to an equal number of up- and downregulated genes (after 48hrs of CHD4 silencing 2,195 genes were upregulated and 2,848 downregulated, while upon 48hrs of P3F silencing 1,827 were upregulated and 1,700 downregulated; false discovery rate - 1%, fold change ≥25%, Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: RNA-seq differential gene expression analysis data.

claim: 541 protein coding genes were co-upregulated upon CHD4 or P3F depletion at 48 hours.
source: At 48hrs, CHD4 silencing influenced the expression of 28% of P3F target genes (541 protein coding genes were co-upregulated upon CHD4 or P3F depletion and 449 were co-downregulated, Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: RNA-seq data analysis showing overlap of CHD4 and P3F regulated genes.

claim: 449 protein coding genes were co-downregulated upon CHD4 or P3F depletion at 48 hours.
source: At 48hrs, CHD4 silencing influenced the expression of 28% of P3F target genes (541 protein coding genes were co-upregulated upon CHD4 or P3F depletion and 449 were co-downregulated, Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: RNA-seq data analysis showing overlap of CHD4 and P3F regulated genes.

claim: GSEA ontology analysis confirmed that P3F-enhancer regulated target genes were downregulated upon CHD4 silencing.
source: GSEA ontology analysis performed with the 990 CHD4 and P3F co-regulated genes was able to identify described P3F signatures and confirmed that P3F-enhancer regulated target genes were downregulated upon CHD4 silencing (Figure 5E).
evidence: GSEA analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: CHD4 depletion increased RNA Pol 2 binding at transcription end sites of genes co-upregulated by CHD4 and P3F.
source: This effect was specific to the downregulated genes since similar analysis performed with the co-upregulated genes (n = 541) resulted in an increase in RNA Pol 2 binding at TES (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: ChIP-seq data for RNA Pol 2 after CHD4 knockdown.

claim: The Combined RNAi dataset comprises data from 974 RNAi screens targeting 17,309 genes in 712 cancer cell lines.
source: The combined RNAi dataset comprises data from 974 RNAi screens targeting 17,309 genes in 712 cancer cell lines
evidence: Description of publicly available cancer dependency database.

claim: The CRISPR dataset screened 17,634 genes in 558 cancer cell lines.
source: while the CRISPR dataset screened 17,634 genes in 558 cancer cell lines.
evidence: Description of publicly available cancer dependency database.

claim: In cancer dependency datasets, gene dependency is depicted as a dependency score estimating essentiality on an absolute scale where zero represents non-essentiality.
source: In both datasets, cancer vulnerability is depicted as a dependency score which estimates gene dependency on an absolute scale where zero represents no dependency or non-essentiality.
evidence: Description of how dependency scores are calculated in the databases.

claim: 627 out of 712 cancer cell lines in the Combined RNAi database were sensitive to CHD4 silencing.
source: We observed that loss of CHD4 impaired tumor cell viability in >92% of the cancer cell lines used in both datasets (in the combined RNAi database, 627 out of 712 cancer cell lines were sensitive to CHD4 silencing
evidence: Analysis of Combined RNAi cancer dependency database.

claim: 552 out of 558 cancer cell lines in the CRISPR dataset were affected by CHD4 knockout.
source: and in the CRISPR dataset 552 out of 558 cancer cell lines were affected by CHD4 knockout).
evidence: Analysis of CRISPR cancer dependency database.

claim: Other NuRD members apart from RBBP4 showed only tumor-specific dependencies.
source: Other NuRD members, apart from RBBP4, showed only tumor-specific dependencies (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Analysis of cancer dependency databases for NuRD subunits.

claim: Loss of SRCAP, EP400, INO80 and BRD4 induced a general impairment of tumor cell viability in cancer databases.
source: In both databases loss of SRCAP, EP400, INO80 and BRD4 induced a general impairment of tumor cell viability
evidence: Analysis of cancer dependency databases for chromatin remodelers and BRD4.
